titre: The color print of *Le Voyage dans la Lune* (A Trip to the Moon) resurfaced as a single frozen block
accroche: Found in 1993, the only hand-colored print of Méliès's film had fused entirely into a block of film stock.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1902, the year of its release, *Le Voyage dans la Lune* (A Trip to the Moon) by Georges Méliès can be bought in two versions from the Star Film catalog: a black-and-white print and, for an extra charge, a print colored by hand, frame by frame, by teams of women workers applying aniline dyes with a fine brush. Few color prints can have been produced, and in the years that follow, stenciling gradually replaces this hand craft. For decades, only black-and-white prints of the film circulate: the color version is considered lost.

## A print found, but impossible to unroll

In 1993, an anonymous donation hands over to the Filmoteca de Catalunya, in Barcelona, a collection of two hundred silent films. One of them is a colored print of *Le Voyage dans la Lune*. The flag waved in the departure scene is painted in the colors of Spain, a sign that this print had been made for a Spanish exhibitor. In 1999, the Filmoteca reports its existence to Serge Bromberg and Eric Lange, of the company Lobster Films, who obtain it in exchange for a recently found film by Segundo de Chomón. But the film stock, still on its reel, has fused entirely into a rigid block. Several specialized laboratories then judge any restoration impossible.

Bromberg and Lange take it on themselves and discover that only the edges of the film stock have melted and stuck together: the images, for the most part, remain intact. Starting in 2000, they manage to separate and digitize 13,375 fragments of images. Tom Burton, head of restoration at Technicolor, receives these fragments in no order whatsoever. It will take him and his team nine months to reconstitute the sequence of shots from these pieces, sometimes a mere corner of an image or half of a frame, filling the gaps with the help of a black-and-white print kept by the Méliès family.

## What it shifts

Twelve years and about a million dollars after the discovery of the block of film, the restored version opens the Cannes Film Festival on May 11, 2011, one hundred nine years after the film's release and eighteen years after its rediscovery. What the audience sees is not, strictly speaking, a restored print, in the sense usually meant for a film that is damaged but legible. It is a reconstruction built fragment by fragment from an object that specialists had judged lost a second time. The work, Tom Burton will say, consisted less in restoring a film than in remanufacturing one, shot by shot, from what survived of it only as crumbs.

citation.texte: What we got was a bunch of digital data that had no sequential relationship to each other because they had to photograph whatever frame or piece of a frame that they could. We had to figure out the puzzle of where these chunks of frames, sometimes little corners of a frame or a half of a frame, where all these little pieces went.

carte.punch: The only color print of *Le Voyage dans la Lune* was found fused into a block of film stock.
carte.idee: In 1902, Méliès's *Le Voyage dans la Lune* also existed in a hand-colored print. Considered lost, it resurfaces in 1993, fused entirely into a rigid block. It will take eighteen years and about a million dollars to digitize and reassemble 13,375 fragments, frame by frame.

quiz.question: In what condition did Serge Bromberg and Eric Lange find the color print of *Le Voyage dans la Lune* in 1999?
choix: Fused into a single rigid block of film stock, to a degree that several laboratories judged beyond repair
Intact, but stored by mistake in the archives of another Méliès film
Cut into hundreds of short fragments already carefully labeled by a previous restorer
Converted into a black-and-white negative by a Spanish laboratory in the 1930s
quiz.explication: The film stock had fused into a rigid block that several specialized laboratories judged impossible to restore. Bromberg and Lange had to separate the fragments themselves, discovering that only the edges had melted and that most of the images were still usable.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How were colored prints of *Le Voyage dans la Lune* made in 1902?
choix: By an automatic chemical dye bath, with no manual intervention
By hand, frame by frame, by women workers applying aniline dyes with a brush
By projecting colored light synchronized during the screening in the theater
By superimposing a second, tinted film stock on the original black-and-white stock
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text specifies that the colored print was made frame by frame by teams of women workers applying aniline dyes with a fine brush, before stenciling replaced this work.

quiz_supplementaire.question: In exchange for what did the Filmoteca de Catalunya hand over the colored print to Lobster Films in 1999?
choix: A sum of about a million dollars, paid directly to the institution
The promise of a free restoration of its entire collection of silent films
A recently found film by Segundo de Chomón
Exclusive broadcast rights to *Le Voyage dans la Lune* for ten years
quiz_supplementaire.explication: In 1999, the Filmoteca reports the print's existence to Bromberg and Lange, of Lobster Films, who obtain it in exchange for a recently found film by Segundo de Chomón.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did Tom Burton's team use to fill in the missing fragments during the reconstruction?
choix: A black-and-white print kept by the Méliès family
Original preparatory drawings by Georges Méliès found in 2005
A colored print kept by a second American private collector
Set photographs published in the press of the time
quiz_supplementaire.explication: To fill the gaps between the fragments that were found, the Technicolor team relied on a black-and-white print of the film kept by the Méliès family.
